3|# Handoff 02 - claude: framing panel B - the event-driven watch, and a browser engine inside C3
4|
5|Date: 2026-10-14. Base commit: C3 `v0.2.1` (8a133f8). C3 is a Rust bridge that lets a coordinating agent (Claude
6|Code first; Codex CLI and other hosts through the same skills) consult reviewer models through their CLIs
7|(engines: codex, agy for Gemini, muse for Meta's Muse Code, http for OpenRouter/API models) with a roster, a
8|findings store, detached runs and panels. Read `README.md`, `plugin/skills/coordinate/SKILL.md` (the waiting rule)
9|and `docs/port/wave8-quota.md`.
10|
11|## Question
12|
13|Two designs before implementation. (A) The WATCH: a coordinator session waits for workers, detached panels, builds
14|and peer sessions by a wake every 20-30 minutes that keeps its prompt cache warm; most wakes find nothing and still
15|cost a full cached read of a large context. We want an event-driven watch inside the bridge that answers "did
16|anything change since <instant>?" so a wake can be skipped or answered in one line without reading the context.
17|(B) A BROWSER ENGINE: reviewers that exist only as web chats (through the user's own Chrome tab, user-land
18|adapters) as a C3 engine beside codex/agy/muse/http - the product rules are already decided by the operator (below);
19|the panel is asked about the architecture inside C3.
20|
21|## Task state
22|
23|- Done: detached runs and panels with `--status` / `--wait`; the waiting rule in the coordinate skill (a wake about
24|  every 20 minutes via the host's scheduler, small reads at each wake, an idle rule after two quiet wakes); the
25|  SessionStart hook line.
26|- Open (A): nothing in the bridge knows whether a wake is useful; the host's scheduler (Claude Code: a cron-like
27|  prompt, `ScheduleWakeup`, a `Monitor` on a file) can only fire or not fire.
28|- Open (B): no engine for web-only reviewers; the operator's rulings (from a panel of 2026-10-14 in the plugin
29|  repository, ROADMAP.md "Browser engine"): nothing site-specific in the product; adapters compiled to WASM from
30|  Rust as the primary form, JavaScript allowed behind ONE deny-by-default host API; draft-only by default (the
31|  adapter prepares, the user sends); pacing is rate limiting, never stealth jitter; a signed hash/pointer catalogue
32|  of adapters; a private plugin first; the public usefulness table ranks per adapter and vendor.
33|- Not in scope: the host's scheduler itself; any site-specific adapter; the measurement designs (panel A).
34|
35|## Evidence
36|
37|- `crates/c3/src/consult/detach.rs`, `crates/c3-cli/src/main.rs` (`--status`, `--wait`) - the status files a
38|  watch could fold.
39|- `plugin/skills/coordinate/SKILL.md` - the waiting rule as written for Claude Code (ScheduleWakeup ~1200 s).
40|- `crates/c3/src/engines/{codex.rs,subprocess.rs}` - the engine contract today: a CLI spawned with a prompt on
41|  stdin, a structured reply by output schema, a transcript, liveness and kill records (the recovery chain that the
42|  acceptance rounds hardened: "no kill without a record").
43|- `~/gemini-mcp` (the operator's prior art, outside this repository): a Chrome extension plus a WebSocket relay that
44|  drove a web chat from an MCP server.
45|
46|## The coordinator's sketch (to be challenged)
47|
48|(A) `c3 watch --task <t> --since <instant> [--worker-state <path>...]`: reads the status files of detached runs,
49|the tails of the named worker STATE files, the ledger's newest entry and the health journal, and prints ONE line:
50|`nothing since <instant> (next known event: <detached run budget end / quota reset>)` or `changed: <what>` - exit
51|code 0 nothing, 3 changed. The host's wake then runs this command first (a few hundred tokens) and reads the context
52|only on exit 3; a Monitor on the status directory can replace the periodic wake entirely where the host has one. A
53|`--next` hint lets the coordinator schedule the next wake at the earliest known event instead of a fixed period.
54|
55|(B) An engine `browser` with the same contract as the others (brief in, structured reply out, transcript, kill
56|record): C3 starts a local relay (WebSocket, loopback only, a per-run token), the Chrome extension connects, an
57|ADAPTER (WASM, loaded from the signed catalogue by hash) runs inside the extension with a host API of a few calls
58|(open the chat URL, put text in the composer, read the reply stream, done) that is deny-by-default per capability;
59|default mode draft-only: C3 writes the brief into the composer and the user presses send; `--send` lets the adapter
60|send when the user allowed it once for that adapter; pacing by a token bucket per vendor; the reply is parsed by
61|the output schema like the others; the usefulness table keys on adapter + vendor.
62|
63|## Alternatives weighed
64|
65|1. **(A) the watch command + `--next` hint (the sketch)** - small; the host still has to fire the wake.
66|2. **(A) a long-lived `c3 serve` that pushes events** (a local socket the host's Monitor can read) - no wasted
67|   wakes at all; a daemon to keep alive and secure.
68|3. **(B) WASM adapters in the extension (the sketch)** vs **(B') the adapter runs in C3 and the extension is a dumb
69|   DOM bridge** (the host API is then C3's, the extension is tiny and auditable) vs **(B'') a Chrome DevTools
70|   Protocol driver without an extension** (no user-land install; fragile, against the "user's own tab" ruling).
71|
72|Current preference: (A) 1 now, 2 later; (B) B' - the extension as a dumb, signed DOM bridge; the adapters as WASM
73|in C3's process with the deny-by-default host API there.
74|
75|## Questions
76|
77|- **Q1.** (A) What should the watch fold, and what is the cheapest reliable "next known event" the coordinator can
78|  schedule against? Where does a skipped wake lose something (a cache that expires, a worker that died silently)?
79|- **Q2.** (B) Where should the adapter run - the extension (WASM), C3's process (B'), or elsewhere - given the
80|  rulings (deny-by-default host API, draft-only, signed catalogue)? What is the minimal host API?
81|- **Q3.** (B) What must the engine record for the recovery chain (liveness, kill, a reply that never comes because
82|  the user did not press send)?
83|- **Q4.** A risk or a design we did not list, for either.
84|
85|Answer by number. Keep it under 600 words.

8|
9|# Coordinate (c3)
10|
11|The C3 port supports one coordinator host: **Claude Code**. This skill is the coordination
12|layer over the `c3` binary. (The multi-host coordination story — Codex CLI, Z Code, Kimi Code,
13|a plain shell — stays with the `codex-consult` PowerShell bridge and is deliberately not ported
14|here.) The consultation procedure itself is the `consult` skill; wiring reviewers is
15|`setup-providers`.
16|
17|## Invariants
18|
19|- **You are the coordinator and the judge by default.** Workers execute, reviewers advise, you
20|  decide and verify. Never redo a worker's work once it reports — read the report and verify in
21|  your own loop; what still needs checking is a new, scoped task.
22|- **One objective per worker.** Brief it precisely the first time: the objective, the exact
23|  files, the numbers its result is measured against, what it must not touch, the report shape. A
24|  launch, a wait and a re-brief cost more than a brief written once.
25|- **English to reviewers and workers.** Briefs, prompts and handoff titles are in English;
26|  source material in another language is translated or summarised, never pasted.
27|- **Wait without blocking; keep the prompt cache warm.** Poll a state file or `c3 consult --task
28|  <task> --status`; never sit in a blocking foreground wait longer than the shell tool's limit.
29|  After the cache's lifetime the next request re-writes the whole context, so a large context
30|  must not go cold by oversight.
31|  - *Running work* (keeps the wake armed, idle count zero): a worker or subagent that has not
32|    reported; a detached consultation or panel (start `c3 consult --task <task> --wait` in the
33|    background - its exit is the signal - or poll `--status`); a long shell job (a suite, a
34|    build); a window you gave another session, until it says it is done; an operator step with a
35|    named end ("I install it and come back"); a cooldown with a named end (a provider's
36|    `retry_after`, a quota window). Idle is only: none of these, and nothing can be done without
37|    the operator.
38|  - *The means in Claude Code:* a Monitor or a background wait is the primary signal; the
39|    `ScheduleWakeup` tool is the heartbeat - about 20 minutes (1200 s), armed at the first
40|    delegation or wait of the session and kept while running work goes on. Every wake: small
41|    reads only (a state file's tail, `c3 consult --task <task> --status`); one line when nothing
42|    finished. Anything finished or needing action is activity: act, and the idle count restarts.
43|  - *Idle:* idle wake 1 - one line in the state file ("idle since <time>"); idle wake 2 - write
44|    the handover on disk, stop the wakeups, and tell the operator in one line the cheap ways
45|    back: a fresh session from the state file; `/compact` is the operator's to run.
46|  - *Compaction* only at a wave boundary (the report is read, the state is on disk) and only
47|    while the cache is warm. In Claude Code the agent has no means to compact itself: while work
48|    runs, keep the context warm however long the wait; when idle, hand over as above.
49|- **Rate every consultation** once its reply is read (`c3 findings --task <task> --rate <n>
50|  --useful yes|partly|no`). A routed panel draws its seats from these marks.
51|- **Ask the operator before going on without a required reviewer** — when one the topic needs is
52|  out, or `--require` refuses the run, tell the operator who is out and until when.
53|
54|## The live-member rule
55|
56|While an `agy` or `muse` member runs (a single run or a panel member, detached or not), write
57|NOTHING under the collab directory or the working tree — `state.md`, notes and findings stores
58|included — and run no git command. Both engines are checked by evidence: a change during an
59|`agy` run FAILS that member; during a `muse` run it WARNS; either way the reviewer read a moving
60|target. This binds your workers too: hold a writing worker until `--status` says the run is
61|done, then write what you queued. (The `http` engine never touches the machine — it only warns.)
62|
63|## The coordinator record
64|
65|- The coordinator's session identity never reaches a reviewer child. `c3` scrubs the host
66|  markers (`CODEX_SESSION_ID`, the `CLAUDE_CODE_*` session ids, the messaging socket and token,
67|  `CLAUDE_PID`, `CLAUDE_EFFORT`, every `CODEX_SANDBOX*`, and the `ZCODE_*` / `ZCODE_PLUGIN*`)
68|  from every reviewer CLI and launcher probe. The ledger records the removed NAMES in
69|  `child_env_scrubbed`, never a value. The operator's own settings, the plugin roots and the
70|  provider keys are kept.
71|- The coordinator's identity is recorded once per run in the ledger `coordinator`
72|  `{provider, model, engine, host, source}`. `host` is `claude-code` when the Claude Code
73|  markers are present, else `unknown`. Set `CODEX_CONSULT_COORDINATOR` to `<provider> :: <model>`
74|  (optionally ` [<engine>]`), a roster position `#<n>` or a provider label to name the
75|  coordinator's own model; a reviewer the bridge seats that IS your model gets a warning (never a
76|  refusal), and an unparseable value is refused before anything starts. Keep the operator's value
77|  when it is set — do not guess your own.
78|
79|## The bridge's own background means
80|
81|Prefer these to the host's own backgrounding. Full mechanics and exit codes: the `consult`
82|skill's `reference.md`.
83|
84|- `c3 consult --detach ...` — run a consultation or a panel in the background, return at once
85|  with the detach id, its status file and the come-back commands. Checked first: a refusal comes
86|  back immediately, nothing written.
87|- `c3 consult --task <task> --status [--id <id>]` — read status only, never blocks (0 done+usable,
88|  1 done with a failure or died, 2 running). `--status --prune` removes files of runs done/died
89|  > 7 days.
90|- `c3 consult --task <task> --wait [--id <id>] [--wait-timeout-sec <s>]` — block until done; keep
91|  `<s>` below your tool's command timeout.
92|- `c3 consult --task <task> --kick --member <NN> [--id <id>]` — stop ONE hung member; its partial
93|  is salvaged and the panel goes on. Ask the operator before kicking a merely-slow member.
94|
95|Park a detached run in the task's `state.md` (the detach id, the brief path, the come-back
96|command); a later session finds it there and in the SessionStart line.
97|
98|**Quota windows (wave 8).** Before a wave of reviews on a subscription plan, read the QUOTA column of
99|`c3 providers` (`5h 96% until 18:32; wk 15% until Oct 20`): a quota window at 98 % or more makes
100|the reviewer out until its reset, like a usage limit - ask the operator whether to wait or to go on
101|without that reviewer. Keep review threads small: prefer `--mode new` with a brief that names the
102|earlier reply over forking a large thread (a parent rollout over `CODEX_CONSULT_FORK_MAX_KB` is refused,
103|it would be replayed on every tool call); the bridge stops a run at `--budget` (90 % by default) with its
104|partial kept, and turns the reviewer's sub-agents off.
105|
106|## Supporting c3 commands
107|
108|- `c3 pack --brief <b> --out <o> [--focus <glob>] [--budget <n>] [--task <t>]` — build a
109|  sanitizing reviewer pack (with a `.pack.json` sidecar) for the `http` engine or for a chat
110|  model; the index feeds the periphery when present, else a lexical neighbourhood.
111|- `c3 explain --claim "<c>" [--focus <glob>] [--audience <who>] --yes` — an explainer pack for
112|  one claim. **It leaves the machine only after you confirm** (`--yes` skips the prompt).
113|- `c3 snapshot [--delta] [--depth 0-9] [--budget <n>] [--focus <glob>]` — a repository snapshot,
114|  optionally a git delta since the last full snapshot's anchor.
115|- `c3 index build|rebuild|query|stats` — the local code index (embedded SurrealDB, per project).
116|  Never required for a consultation; `query` is BM25 + reciprocal-rank with a bounded 1-hop
117|  expansion.
118|- `c3 router simulate|replay|priors|explain` — routing insight: `explain` prints the score table
119|  the next panel draw would use, one line per roster lineage; `replay` confirms a routed panel's
120|  seats from the ledger.

The brief frames (A) as poll-vs-push and (B) as where-to-run-the-adapter, but both inherit harder constraints. For (A), the wake itself is the cost: the host must still fire to run `watch`, so the design saves context re-reads, not wakes, and every skipped wake trades cache warmth for savings — a cold cache re-reads everything anyway. Unlisted options: a host-native file Monitor as the primary signal with wake only as fallback; a background waiter that writes a wake file; folding at most status mtimes/ledger seq rather than tails of free-form worker STATE files. For (B), treating a user-tab chat as "the same contract as the others" is the framing risk: no spawn/kill/timeout semantics, unbounded human latency, auth/CAPTCHA/ToS breakage, and draft text crossing a trust boundary. Unlisted options: browser as pack-consumer plus human-pasted reply (no engine at all); a sidecar outside C3 core behind the private plugin; explicitly non-goal: full auto-send. To choose I would need: wake token cost vs cold re-read cost and cache lifetime; which hosts actually offer Monitor/file-watch; per-run token/audit requirements for the relay; and who owns adapter-selector breakage.

## Q1 — what should watch fold, cheapest reliable next event, what skipping loses

Fold only locally-authored, monotonic facts: detached status-file mtime+state transitions, ledger sequence, named worker-state mtimes, health-journal entries C3 wrote. Do not parse STATE tails or quota text for change detection. The only reliable "next" is the earliest locally-known deadline: detached budget end or member timeout. Quota reset is advisory (shared, moves without us — finding #2). A skipped wake loses two things: cache warmth (skip too many and the re-read costs more than the wakes saved — cap consecutive skips) and silent death (a worker that died without writing looks identical to "nothing changed"; the watch must distinguish "no evidence" from "evidence of nothing" and age out the former).

## Q2 — where should the adapter run, minimal host API

Prefer B': dumb signed DOM bridge in the extension, adapters in C3 — but only because audit, catalogue-pin, and consent live better in C3, not because it removes selector fragility (finding #4). Minimal API is not open/compose/read/done; it is: bind(tab, origin, run-token), checkCatalogueHash, putDraft, readStream, reportDone, appendAudit, revoke. Deny-by-default per capability, consent per adapter-hash (an update re-asks), loopback-only relay with per-run token and origin pin.

## Q3 — what the engine must record

New states, not the subprocess chain: prepared / awaiting-user / sent / streaming / abandoned, plus relay-liveness heartbeats. Kill becomes token-revoke; add explicit expire/abandon owned by the coordinator (`--kick` abandons the draft). Record adapter hash + vendor + draft-vs-sent + abandon reason; keep drafts and digests out of telemetry (closed outcome classes only). Unsent-across-N-wakes must have a defined expiry, and tab-close/relay-drop must map to a status-file state, never to silent running.

## Q4 — unlisted risk/design

Silent narrowing: a watch that answers in one line becomes the coordinator's only eyes, so a stale/broken watch (clock skew, pruned status files, full disk) fails closed to "nothing" and idles the session into handover. Design the watch to fail loud (unknown exit distinct from nothing/changed) and to print its cursor so the next wake can audit it. For the browser engine: version the usefulness key by adapter hash, and treat `--send` as the product's riskiest surface — rate limiting is not consent.
